title: Alone or Together?
blurb: Talk about housing and living arrangements

steps.html:
Twenty households in Leeds share one laundry and a garden. Forty-seven per cent of Swedish homes contain exactly one person. Two texts about how we live, and the small words that decide whether you mean few or a few.

  • Read two texts about housing and compare their arguments
  • Use few / a few, most of, neither of, plenty of accurately
  • Describe numbers and proportions in words
  • Write about how people live where you are

steps.title: Text A · The room used nine nights a year
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the UK Cohousing Network and published research on Danish cohousing.

Most of the houses built in Europe over the last century contain a room that is used for about nine nights a year. A few families use the spare bedroom more than that; hardly any use it enough to justify heating it, cleaning it and paying a mortgage on it. Multiply that by every household in a neighbourhood and the waste stops looking like a private eccentricity and starts looking like a planning problem.

Co-housing starts from exactly this observation. Each family owns or rents a private property, with its own kitchen and its own front door, and every resident can shut that door on the rest of the world. What the households do not each own is a guest room, a laundry, a workshop or an entertainment space. There is one of each, shared, and both the cost and the cleaning are divided among all of them. The private dwellings are usually smaller than average on purpose, because the money saved goes into the common house instead.

Neither the idea nor the arithmetic is new. The first modern scheme opened north of Copenhagen in 1972, after its architect’s earlier attempt had collapsed in the face of neighbours’ objections; twenty-seven households moved in, and a second Danish project followed a year later. Several hundred communities now exist across northern Europe, and the Netherlands alone has more than three hundred. Most of them were designed by the people who were going to live in them, which is slow, and which is also the point: residents who have argued for two years about where to put the bins tend to know their neighbours.

steps.title: Text B · What the research actually finds
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Choi, European Planning Studies (2004) and comparative studies of senior cohousing in Denmark and the Netherlands.

What has changed is who applies. Most of the early residents were young families looking for somewhere the children could be watched by more than two adults. A large number of applicants now are people over seventy who want to go on living independently, in a property they control, and who know perfectly well what the alternative looks like. Studies of senior schemes in Denmark, Sweden and the Netherlands report the same finding: the dominant motive is not practical help but the avoidance of isolation. Several of them also record higher levels of social and physical activity among residents than among comparable people living alone.

None of this suits everybody, and the literature is honest about that. Some of the meetings are long, and a few of them are about washing machines. Decisions taken by consensus can take months. Residents eat separately most nights, and plenty of them say the shared meals are the part they would give up first. Cohousing also tends to attract people with time, confidence and a university education, which limits how far it can be offered as a general answer to anything.

But almost all of them mention the same thing, and it is not the guest room. Somebody notices when your curtains stay shut. In a period that has seen a steady rise in one-person households across Europe, and growth in the number of people studying and working at home through distance learning, that is not a small claim. The spare bedroom was never really the problem. It was the clearest sign of a way of building that assumed everyone would rather be left alone.

steps.title: How much, how many, and how you feel about it
steps.html:
The full picture, then the two distinctions that decide B2 accuracy.

Some quantifiers go only with countable nouns (many, few, a few, several, a number of), some only with uncountable (much, little, a little, a great deal of), and some with either (a lot of, plenty of, most, some, no, all).

The first distinction: few against a few. A few means 'some, and that is a reasonable number'. Few means 'almost none', and it carries a negative judgement. The same applies to little and a little: a little time is enough, little time is not.

The second: of or no of. Use of only when you are talking about a specific, already-identified group: most of the residents, few of them. With a general statement, drop it: most residents, few people.

Each, every, neither, either, none are singular and take a singular verb: Each of them explains some of it. None of them explains all of it. Neither of the two families was able to sell.

For describing data, the usual phrases are the majority of, a significant proportion of, roughly a third of, just under half of, almost nobody.

Nine floors, one lift

Most of the flats in my building were bought in the 1990s, and a great many of them are still lived in by the same families. That is unusual now. Few of my friends have stayed anywhere for more than four years.

A few of my neighbours know each other well — the four women on the second floor have been organising the courtyard for decades. Plenty of people, though, have never spoken to anybody above the fifth floor. Neither of the families next to me was here when I moved in.

Roughly a third of the flats now have one resident, which would have been unthinkable to my grandmother. Almost nobody I know under thirty lives with their parents once they are working, and very few of them plan to.
